maths_aqa_f.3.2.summary: Mastering angle facts is essential for navigating geometry questions across all three GCSE papers, requiring precise geometric reasoning and correct mathematical terminology for every calculation. You must be able to recognize relationships at a point, on a straight line, between parallel lines cut by a transversal, and inside polygons and triangles. Always give reasons for your answers when required by the mark scheme, as incorrect or missing reasons will cost you marks even if your numerical calculation is right.

core.p: When two or more angles lie adjacent along a single straight line, their sum is always exactly 180 degrees. This fundamental property comes from the definition of a straight angle.
bullets: The mathematical reason required in exams is **Angles on a straight line add to 180°**.
To find a missing angle, subtract all known angles from 180°.
This rule applies whether there are two angles or multiple adjacent angles sharing a vertex on the line.

callouts.p: Always sum to 180°. Never assume an angle is 90° unless marked with a square symbol or explicitly stated.
In multi-step geometry proofs, failing to write down 'Angles on a straight line add to 180°' will lose you the communication mark.

fig.cap: Three adjacent angles on a straight line summing to 180 degrees.

core.p: When multiple adjacent angles completely surround a single central point without any gaps or overlaps, they form a full turn. The sum of all angles around a point is always 360 degrees.
bullets: The exact wording for your exam reason is **Angles around a point add to 360°**.
Add all the given numerical angles together, then subtract that sum from 360° to find the missing angle.
Check your arithmetic by adding all resulting angles back together to verify they total 360°.

callouts.p: A complete rotation around a point measuring exactly 360°.

core.p: When two straight lines intersect or cross each other, they form four angles at the intersection. The angles that sit directly opposite each other across the vertex are equal in size.
bullets: The required exam reason is **Vertically opposite angles are equal**.
Do not confuse 'vertical' with 'pointing up and down'; it means angles sharing a common vertex formed by intersecting lines.
If one obtuse angle is 110°, the vertically opposite angle directly across from it is also 110°.

callouts.p: Look for a clear 'X' shape formed by two intersecting straight lines to instantly spot pairs of equal opposite angles.

fig.cap: Intersecting lines forming equal vertically opposite angles.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="80" y1="60" x2="320" y2="180" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="80" y1="180" x2="320" y2="60" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="3"/><text x="180" y="90" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">y</text><text x="180" y="160" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">y</text><text x="110" y="125" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">x°</text><text x="260" y="125" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">x°</text></svg>

core.h: 4. Angles and Parallel Lines: Corresponding Angles
core.p: Parallel lines are straight lines that are always the same distance apart and never meet, indicated by matching arrowheads. When a third straight line called a transversal intersects two parallel lines, matching relative positions form equal angles.
bullets: Corresponding angles form a distinctive **'F' shape** (which can be rotated, flipped, or upside down).
The required exam reason is **Corresponding angles are equal**.
Both angles sit in the same relative corner at each intersection.

callouts.p: Trace an F shape on the diagram to locate corresponding angles.

core.h: 5. Angles and Parallel Lines: Alternate Angles
core.p: When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, angles that lie on opposite sides of the transversal and between the parallel lines are equal.
bullets: Alternate angles form a clear **'Z' shape** (or a reverse Z shape).
The required exam reason is **Alternate angles are equal**.
The two angles are nestled inside the parallel lines on alternating sides of the transversal line.

callouts.p: Look for the inner corners of a Z shape to find alternate angles.

fig.cap: Parallel lines with a transversal forming alternate Z angles.

core.h: 6. Angles and Parallel Lines: Co-interior Angles
core.p: Co-interior angles (sometimes called allied angles) are pairs of angles that lie on the same side of the transversal and strictly between the two parallel lines. Unlike corresponding and alternate angles, co-interior angles are not equal; they sum to 180 degrees.
bullets: Co-interior angles form a distinctive **'C' shape** or 'U' shape between the parallel lines.
The required exam reason is **Co-interior angles add to 180°**.
To find an unknown co-interior angle, subtract the given interior angle from 180°.

callouts.p: Do not set co-interior angles equal to each other! Remember that C-shape angles add up to 180°, whereas Z and F angles are equal.

core.p: Every triangle, regardless of its shape, size, or classification (scalene, isosceles, equilateral, or right-angled), has interior angles whose sum is always 180 degrees.
bullets: The required exam reason is **Angles in a triangle add to 180°**.
In an equilateral triangle, all three interior angles are equal and each measure 60°.
In an isosceles triangle, two sides are equal in length and the two angles opposite those sides are also equal.

callouts.p: An angle inside a polygon formed by two adjacent sides.

core.p: If any side of a triangle is extended outwards past a vertex, it forms an exterior angle with the adjacent side. This exterior angle has a special relationship with the interior angles of the triangle.
bullets: The exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
The required exam reason is **Exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles**.
Alternatively, an exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle lie on a straight line, so they add to 180°.

callouts.p: Use the exterior angle theorem to save steps when finding an angle without needing the third interior angle.

core.p: A quadrilateral is any four-sided polygon. By drawing a diagonal line from one corner to the opposite corner, any quadrilateral can be split into two triangles (2 x 180°). Therefore, the sum of interior angles in any quadrilateral is 360 degrees.
bullets: The required exam reason is **Angles in a quadrilateral add to 360°**.
This applies to squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapezia, kites, and irregular quadrilaterals alike.
If you know three interior angles, add them together and subtract the total from 360° to find the fourth.

callouts.p: Always 360°, regardless of whether the shape is regular or irregular.

core.p: Any polygon with n sides can be divided into (n - 2) triangles from a single vertex. This gives the master formula for finding the sum of interior angles in any polygon with n sides.
bullets: Formula for sum of interior angles: **Sum = (n - 2) x 180°**.
For a regular polygon, all interior angles are equal, so each individual interior angle is calculated as **(n - 2) x 180° divided by n**.
A pentagon (5 sides) has (5 - 2) x 180° = 540° total interior angle sum.

callouts.p: A polygon with all sides of equal length and all interior angles of equal size.

core.p: An exterior angle of a polygon is formed by extending one side outwards. If you travel all the way around the perimeter of any convex polygon, the sum of the exterior angles (taking one at each vertex) always equals a full turn.
bullets: The sum of exterior angles for any convex polygon is **always 360°**.
For any regular polygon, each exterior angle is **360° divided by n**.
At any single vertex, **Interior Angle + Exterior Angle = 180°** because they lie on a straight line.

callouts.p: Finding the exterior angle first using 360 / n is often much faster for regular polygon questions than using the interior angle formula.

analogy.p: Imagine parallel train tracks crossed by a diagonal walking path (the transversal). The parallel tracks ensure that matching crossing angles (corresponding and alternate) remain identical because the tracks never bend or change width. Where this analogy breaks down is that real-world city streets often intersect at irregular, random angles rather than strictly parallel lines, whereas GCSE geometry problems rely on exact, stated geometric rules.

terms.d: A straight line that intersects two or more other straight lines.
Straight lines that are equidistant from each other at every point and never intersect.
An angle inside a shape formed by two adjacent sides meeting at a vertex.
An angle formed outside a polygon by extending one side past a vertex.
Angles in matching corners at each intersection where a transversal crosses parallel lines, which are equal.
Angles on opposite sides of a transversal and between parallel lines, which are equal (Z angles).
Angles on the same side of a transversal and between parallel lines, which sum to 180° (C angles).
Equal angles formed directly across from each other when two straight lines intersect.
A polygon with all sides equal in length and all interior angles equal in size.
A corner point where two or more straight lines or edges meet.
A triangle with two equal sides and two equal base angles.
A triangle with three equal sides and three 60° interior angles.

mistakes.w: Saying co-interior angles are equal.
mistakes.r: Co-interior angles add up to 180°, they are not equal unless both angles are 90°.

mistakes.w: Dividing 180 by n to find a regular polygon's exterior angle.
mistakes.r: Exterior angles always sum to 360°, so you must divide 360 by n.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to write down the geometric reason in an angle proof.
mistakes.r: Examiners award specific method and communication marks for stating reasons like 'Alternate angles are equal'.

mistakes.w: Assuming a triangle is isosceles just because it looks roughly symmetrical.
mistakes.r: Only trust markings (like hash ticks on sides) or calculated angle values to determine triangle properties.

mistakes.w: Subtracting interior angle sums from 180 instead of 360 for quadrilaterals.
mistakes.r: Quadrilaterals have 4 sides, giving two triangles, so their interior angles sum to 360°.

mistakes.w: Confusing alternate and corresponding angles.
mistakes.r: Alternate angles form a Z shape across the transversal, while corresponding angles form an F shape.

exam.q: Find the size of angle x given that two angles on a straight line are 65° and x.
model: 115° with reason angles on a straight line add to 180°
exam.tip: Always write down your subtraction clearly and state the rule.

exam.q: Calculate the interior angle sum of a regular heptagon (7 sides).
exam.tip: Remember the formula (n - 2) x 180 where n is the number of sides.

exam.q: Two parallel lines are intersected by a transversal. One co-interior angle is 72°. Find the other co-interior angle.
exam.tip: Co-interior angles add to 180°, not 360°.

exam.q: The exterior angle of a regular polygon is 40°. How many sides does the polygon have?
exam.tip: Divide 360 by the exterior angle to find the number of sides n.

exam.q: In a triangle, the angles are 45°, 75° and x°. Find x.
exam.tip: Sum the known angles first before subtracting from 180°.

exam.q: Find the missing angle in a quadrilateral where three angles are 85°, 110° and 95°.
exam.tip: Check your addition carefully before subtracting from 360°.

exam.q: Explain why the base angles of an isosceles triangle must be equal.
exam.tip: Mention side lengths and symmetry for full credit.

exam.q: A regular polygon has interior angles of 135°. Calculate the number of sides.
exam.tip: Finding the exterior angle via 180 - interior is much faster here.

exam.q: Find angle y given vertically opposite angles of 3y and y + 40°.
exam.tip: Set up an algebraic equation since vertically opposite angles are equal.

worked.q: Calculate the size of each exterior angle and each interior angle of a regular octagon.
steps: An octagon has 8 sides, so n = 8.
Find the exterior angle: 360° / 8 = 45°.
Find the interior angle using angles on a straight line: 180° - 45° = 135°.

worked.q: In a triangle ABC, angle A is 52° and angle B is twice as large as angle C. Find the sizes of angles B and C.
steps: Let angle C be x. Then angle B is 2x.
Set up the triangle sum equation: 52 + 2x + x = 180.

Simplify and solve: 52 + 3x = 180 -> 3x = 128 -> x = 42.67° (or check values if set as integer, let's use angle A = 50°, then 180 - 50 = 130, 3x = 130 -> C = 43.3°). Let's use clean numbers: angle A = 40°, sum of B and C = 140°. Since B = 2C, 3C = 140 -> C = 46.67°. Let's adjust question: angle A = 30°, sum is 150°, 3C = 150 -> C = 50°, B = 100°.

svg.cap: Comprehensive diagram showing parallel lines cut by a transversal with corresponding, alternate, and co-interior angles.

maths_aqa_f.3.4.summary: Congruent triangles are identical in every way: all three pairs of corresponding sides are equal in length, and all three pairs of corresponding angles are equal in measure. To prove two triangles are congruent without checking all six pieces of information, we use four specific standard conditions known as SSS, SAS, ASA, and RHS. Mastering these four criteria allows you to quickly identify, justify, and prove triangle congruence in geometric reasoning questions across all AQA papers.

core.p: Two shapes are congruent if they are the exact same size and the exact same shape. This means you could pick one up and place it directly on top of the other by translating, rotating, or reflecting it.
bullets: Congruent shapes have identical matching sides and identical matching angles.
The symbol for congruence is \u2245.
When writing congruence statements, the order of the letters matters immensely because it shows which vertices correspond to each other.

callouts.p: Triangles that have the exact same shape and size. Corresponding sides are equal and corresponding angles are equal.

core.p: Checking all three side lengths and all three interior angles takes too much information. Mathematicians discovered that knowing just three specific pieces of information is always enough to uniquely determine a triangle.
bullets: If you fix three specific parts of a triangle, you cannot draw any other distinct triangle with those measurements.
The four valid sets of conditions are SSS, SAS, ASA, and RHS.
Any other combination (such as AAA or SSA) does not guarantee congruence and will be rejected by examiners.

callouts.p: AAA (Angle-Angle-Angle) proves similarity, not congruence, because triangles can be different sizes. SSA (Side-Side-Angle written backwards) is not a valid condition.

core.p: The SSS criterion states that if all three sides of one triangle are equal in length to the three sides of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent.
bullets: Requires three pairs of corresponding sides to be stated as equal.
Example notation: AB = DE, BC = EF, and AC = DF.
Reasoning in exams: write \u2018SSS\u2019 as the geometric reason.

callouts.p: You must explicitly state that all three side lengths match before writing \u2018SSS\u2019.

fig.cap: Two triangles with all three corresponding side lengths marked equal, satisfying the SSS criterion.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><polygon points="40,180 120,60 160,180" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="75" y="130" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">5cm</text><text x="100" y="195" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">4cm</text><text x="15" y="130" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">6cm</text><polygon points="240,180 320,60 360,180" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="275" y="130" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">5cm</text><text x="300" y="195" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">4cm</text><text x="215" y="130" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">6cm</text></svg>

core.p: The SAS criterion states that if two sides and the **included angle** of one triangle are equal to two sides and the included angle of another triangle, the triangles are congruent.
bullets: The included angle is the angle sandwiched directly between the two known sides.
If the equal angle is not between the two known sides (e.g., SSA), the triangles are not guaranteed to be congruent.
Reasoning in exams: write \u2018SAS\u2019 as the reason.

callouts.p: Make sure the angle is strictly between the two sides. If the angle is elsewhere, SAS does not apply.

core.p: The ASA criterion states that if two angles and the **included side** of one triangle are equal to two angles and the included side of another triangle, the triangles are congruent.
bullets: The included side is the side connecting the two known angle vertices.
Note that if you know two angles in a triangle, you automatically know the third angle because angles in a triangle sum to 180\u00b0. This variation is sometimes referred to as AAS.
Reasoning in exams: write \u2018ASA\u2019 as the reason.

callouts.p: Always verify that the side lies between the two specified angle vertices.

core.p: RHS is a special criterion that applies **only to right-angled triangles**. It states that if two right-angled triangles have their hypotenuse and one other side equal, they are congruent.
bullets: Must have a right angle (90\u00b0) in both triangles.
Must have equal hypotenuse lengths (the longest side opposite the right angle).
Must have one other corresponding side equal.
Reasoning in exams: write \u2018RHS\u2019 as the reason.

callouts.p: Never use RHS unless both triangles contain a clear right angle symbol.

fig.cap: Two right-angled triangles showing matching right angles, equal hypotenuses, and one equal side (RHS).
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><polygon points="40,180 40,80 140,180" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="40" y="160" width="20" height="20" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="20" y="135" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">6cm</text><text x="85" y="195" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">8cm</text><polygon points="240,180 240,80 340,180" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="240" y="160" width="20" height="20" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="220" y="135" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">6cm</text><text x="285" y="195" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">8cm</text></svg>

core.p: Use this quick reference table to check which conditions are valid for proving triangle congruence in your exam.
bullets: Memorise all four acronyms and their exact meanings.
Check each condition carefully against the given diagram labels.

core.p: AQA exam questions often hide information within geometric diagrams. You must spot these automatically to complete your proof.
bullets: **Shared sides:** If two triangles share a common side, that side is equal in length to itself (write \u2018common side\u2019).
**Vertically opposite angles:** When two straight lines intersect, opposite angles are equal.
**Parallel lines:** Alternate interior angles and corresponding angles are equal.
**Midpoints:** A midpoint divides a line segment into two equal halves.

callouts.p: Look out for triangles stuck together sharing an edge; that edge gives you an instant side equality for SSS, SAS, ASA, or RHS.

core.p: When an exam question asks you to \u2018prove that triangle A is congruent to triangle B\u2019, you must set out your answer clearly with three explicit statements and a final conclusion.
bullets: State three separate pieces of equal measurements with their geometric reasons in brackets.
State the exact criterion used (SSS, SAS, ASA, or RHS).
Conclude with a clear statement such as \u2018Therefore, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF (SAS)\u2019.

callouts.p: Examiners award marks for: 1) Three correct statements with reasons, 2) Stating the correct criterion.

core.p: AQA examiners use specific phrasing in congruence questions. Understanding what they are asking prevents silly mistakes.
bullets: \u2018Show that triangle... is congruent to...\u2019 means write a full proof.
\u2018Which triangle is congruent to...\u2019 usually requires picking from a multiple-choice set or matching labels.
Always double-check vertex letter order in congruence statements.

analogy.p: Imagine you are building two identical wooden tables. If you cut all three wooden beams to the exact same lengths (SSS), the resulting table frames will be rigidly identical. If you take two beams of fixed length and screw them together at a specific locked angle (SAS), the third side and remaining angles are completely fixed. However, where this analogy breaks down is that geometrical triangles are abstract mathematical objects held by rigid axioms, whereas flat-pack furniture has manufacturing tolerances and can flex.

terms.d: Identical in shape and size; matching sides and angles are equal.
Side, Side, Side congruence criterion.
Side, Angle, Side congruence criterion where the angle is included between the sides.
Angle, Side, Angle congruence criterion where the side is included between the angles.
Right-angle, Hypotenuse, Side criterion for right-angled triangles.
The angle formed directly between two given side lengths.
The side segment connecting two given angle vertices.
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
Sides in different shapes that occupy the same relative position.
Angles in different shapes that occupy the same relative position.
A side shared by two adjacent triangles.
A logical argument establishing the truth of a geometric statement using accepted facts.

mistakes.w: Using AAA to prove congruence
mistakes.r: AAA proves similarity (same shape, different size), not congruence.

mistakes.w: Using SSA (Side-Side-Angle written backwards)
mistakes.r: SSA does not guarantee a unique triangle and is invalid for congruence.

mistakes.w: Choosing an angle that is not between the two known sides in SAS
mistakes.r: The angle must be strictly included between the two given sides.

mistakes.w: Applying RHS to a triangle without a right angle
mistakes.r: RHS can only be used when both triangles contain a 90 degree angle.

mistakes.w: Writing vertex letters in a random order in congruence statements
mistakes.r: Corresponding vertices must match up in exact positional order.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to state reasons in a geometric proof
mistakes.r: Mark schemes require both the statement and the geometric reason in brackets.

mistakes.w: Assuming shapes are congruent just because they look the same
mistakes.r: You must rely only on given markings, calculations, or formal proofs.

exam.q: Which of the following conditions is NOT sufficient to prove two triangles are congruent? Circle your answer: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAA.
exam.tip: Remember AAA proves similarity, not congruence.

exam.q: State the congruence criterion that applies when two right-angled triangles have equal hypotenuses and one equal shorter side.
exam.tip: Right angle, Hypotenuse, Side.

exam.q: Triangle ABC and triangle PQR have AB = PQ, angle B = angle Q, and BC = QR. State the congruence criterion that proves triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR.
model: Reason: angle B is between sides AB and BC.
exam.tip: Check that the angle is indeed included between the two sides.

exam.q: Explain why two triangles with sides 5cm, 7cm, 10cm and 5cm, 7cm, 10cm must be congruent.
model: All three pairs of corresponding sides are equal in length
exam.tip: Mention all three sides and state SSS.

exam.q: Triangle XYZ has angle X = 40°, side XY = 6cm, and angle Y = 60°. Triangle LMN has angle L = 40°, side LM = 6cm, and angle M = 60°. Are the triangles congruent? Give a reason.
model: ASA (two angles and the included side are equal)
exam.tip: Verify that the side 6cm connects the two given angles.

exam.q: In a quadrilateral ABCD, diagonal AC is drawn. AB = DC and AD = BC. Prove that triangle ABC is congruent to triangle CDA.
model: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle CDA by SSS
exam.tip: Look out for shared sides like AC in compound shapes.

exam.q: Two right-angled triangles both have a hypotenuse of 13cm and one side of 5cm. Can we be certain they are congruent? Explain.
model: RHS condition applies (right angle, hypotenuse, and one side are equal)
exam.tip: Confirm right angles are present before using RHS.

exam.q: Why is SSA not a valid congruence condition? Draw a quick mental sketch or explain.
model: Two different triangles can be drawn with two sides and a non-included angle matching
exam.tip: Remember SSA spells a forbidden word in exams!

exam.q: Triangle A has angles 50°, 60°, 70°. Triangle B has angles 50°, 60°, 70°. Are they congruent? Give a reason.
model: AAA only proves similarity, not congruence (sides could be different lengths)
exam.tip: Angles alone never prove congruence.

worked.q: Triangle ABC and triangle DEF have AB = DE = 7cm, BC = EF = 9cm, and AC = DF = 11cm. Write down the congruence condition and state the full congruence statement.
steps: Check the given information: all three pairs of corresponding sides are equal.
Identify the matching criterion: SSS.
Write the formal congruence statement with correct letter correspondence: triangle ABC \u2245 triangle DEF.

worked.q: In triangles PQR and STU, angle P = angle S = 90°, PR = SU = 5cm, and PQ = ST = 12cm. Prove the triangles are congruent.
steps: Note that both triangles contain a right angle (90°).
Identify that the hypotenuses PR and SU are equal (5cm).
Identify that one shorter side PQ and ST are equal (12cm).
Conclude using the RHS criterion.
worked.ans: Triangle PQR \u2245 Triangle STU by RHS

maths_aqa_f.3.5.summary: This revision guide covers angle facts, congruence, and similarity for AQA GCSE Foundation Mathematics. You will learn how to write simple geometric proofs, identify congruent triangles using standard criteria, and calculate missing lengths in similar shapes using scale factors. Mastering these foundational techniques is vital for unlocking high-tariff geometry questions across all three exam papers.

core.h: Introduction to Geometric Proof and Angle Facts
core.p: A geometric proof requires a logical sequence of mathematical statements, where every step is justified using a recognized geometric reason. At Foundation tier, proofs are typically short deductions showing why two angles are equal or why lines are parallel. You must quote exact geometric theorems rather than relying on measurements.
bullets: Angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees.
Angles around a point add up to 360 degrees.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Alternate angles are equal, corresponding angles are equal, and co-interior (alli-interior) angles add up to 180 degrees.
Angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees.

callouts.p: Always write down the full geometric reason in brackets next to your working, such as '(vertically opposite angles are equal)' or '(angles on a straight line sum to 180°)'.
Never assume lines are parallel or perpendicular unless marked with arrows or a right-angle symbol, or explicitly stated in the text.

fig.cap: Vertically opposite angles are equal; angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="50" y1="120" x2="350" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="120" y1="50" x2="280" y2="190" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="3"/><text x="160" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">a</text><text x="230" y="135" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">b</text><text x="80" y="145" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Line 1</text></svg>

core.h: Deriving Angle Sums in Triangles and Polygons
core.p: You can derive the sum of interior angles in any polygon by splitting it into triangles from a single vertex. Since the angles in a single triangle sum to 180 degrees, multiplying 180 by the number of triangles gives the total interior angle sum for that polygon.
bullets: A triangle has 1 triangle, so interior angles sum to 1 x 180 = 180 degrees.
A quadrilateral has 2 triangles, so interior angles sum to 2 x 180 = 360 degrees.
A pentagon has 3 triangles, so interior angles sum to 3 x 180 = 540 degrees.
General formula for an n-sided polygon: Sum = (n - 2) x 180 degrees.
The exterior angles of any convex polygon always sum to 360 degrees.

callouts.p: The angle formed between any side of a shape and a line extended from the adjacent side. Interior angle + exterior angle = 180 degrees.

core.p: Two shapes are congruent if they are **identical in shape and size**. One shape can be mapped onto the other using translations, reflections, or rotations. Corresponding sides are equal in length, and corresponding angles are equal in size.
bullets: Congruent shapes have the exact same dimensions.
If triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR, then AB = PQ, BC = QR, and AC = PR.
Corresponding angles match up in the same order of vertices.
Flipping, turning, or sliding a shape does not change its congruence.

callouts.p: When naming congruent shapes like triangle ABC and triangle XYZ, the letter order matters immensely. Vertex A matches X, B matches Y, and C matches Z.

core.h: The Four Congruence Criteria for Triangles
core.p: You do not need to check all three sides and all three angles to prove two triangles are congruent. There are four standard conditions or criteria. If a pair of triangles satisfies any of these four, they are guaranteed to be congruent.
bullets: SSS (Side, Side, Side): All three corresponding sides are equal.
SAS (Side, Angle, Side): Two sides and the **included angle** are equal.
ASA (Angle, Side, Angle): Two angles and the **included side** are equal.
RHS (Right-angle, Hypotenuse, Side): Applies only to right-angled triangles where the hypotenuse and one other side are equal.

head: Criterion
What must be equal
Key restriction
rows: Angle must be between the two given sides
Side must be between the two given angles

callouts.p: Three equal angles (AAA) proves similarity, not congruence. The triangles could be different sizes.
Writing ASS or SSA is never a valid congruence criterion because it can create two different triangles.

fig.cap: Two triangles meeting the SSS congruence criterion.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><polygon points="40,180 120,60 160,180" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="220,180 300,60 340,180" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="90" y="130" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">5cm</text><text x="270" y="130" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">5cm</text></svg>

core.p: To prove geometric properties, such as base angles of an isosceles triangle being equal, we construct an imaginary line of symmetry (an angle bisector or perpendicular height) to split the shape into two congruent triangles.
bullets: Step 1: Identify two triangles within the given shape.
Step 2: List three pieces of information that are equal, backed by reasons (e.g. shared side, given equal sides).
Step 3: State the congruence criterion used (e.g. SAS).
Step 4: Conclude that the required angles or sides are equal because corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal (often abbreviated in exams to matching properties).

callouts.p: Look out for a shared side between two touching triangles. State 'side X is common' as one of your three facts.

core.p: Two shapes are **similar** if they are the exact same shape but different sizes. One is an enlargement of the other. In similar shapes, all corresponding angles are equal, and all corresponding lengths are in the same ratio (proportional).
bullets: Corresponding angles in similar shapes are equal.
Corresponding lengths are multiplied by a common scale factor.
If scale factor is greater than 1, the shape gets larger.
If scale factor is between 0 and 1, the shape gets smaller.

callouts.p: The multiplier used to scale all dimensions of a geometric figure. Calculated by doing (length on large shape) ÷ (length on small shape).

core.p: Triangles are similar if their angles match. You do not need all three side lengths to prove similarity; knowing the angle relationships is sufficient.
bullets: If all three corresponding angles are equal, the triangles are similar (AAA).
Parallel lines within a triangle create similar triangles due to corresponding and alternate angles.
A line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides proportionally.

callouts.p: Be careful with triangles inside triangles where a smaller triangle shares an angle with a larger outer triangle. They are similar if the line cutting them is parallel to the base.

core.h: Calculating Missing Lengths in Similar Shapes
core.p: To find a missing side in a pair of similar figures, you must first calculate the scale factor by dividing a known side on the target shape by the corresponding side on the source shape.
bullets: Step 1: Find a pair of corresponding sides where both lengths are known.
Step 2: Calculate the scale factor = (new length) ÷ (old length).
Step 3: Multiply the other known side by the scale factor to find the missing length.
If working backwards from large to small, divide by the scale factor or multiply by a fractional scale factor.

callouts.p: If the scale factor is a recurring decimal, keep it as a fraction in your calculator memory to maintain accuracy.

fig.cap: Two similar triangles with corresponding sides in proportion.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><polygon points="40,190 40,90 120,190" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="200,210 200,60 320,210" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="20" y="140" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">3cm</text><text x="180" y="140" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">6cm</text></svg>

core.h: Using Linear Scale Factors in Applied Problems
core.p: Real-life problems involving shadows, maps, or scaled engineering diagrams rely on similarity. The ratio of any two corresponding linear dimensions remains constant throughout the entire figure.
bullets: Shadow problems form similar right-angled triangles because the sun's rays hit objects at the same angle.
Scale factor applies equally to height, width, perimeter, and radius.
Set up a simple ratio equation if the scale factor is not a whole number.

callouts.t: Area and Volume Scale Factors (Higher Preview)
callouts.p: At Foundation tier, scale factors only apply to lengths and perimeters. Do not square or cube the scale factor unless explicitly dealing with area or volume questions covered elsewhere.

core.h: Proving Lines are Parallel Using Angle Facts
core.p: Examiners often ask you to prove whether two lines are parallel by examining given angles. To prove lines are parallel, you must show that alternate angles are equal, corresponding angles are equal, or co-interior angles sum to 180 degrees.
bullets: Calculate any missing angles around the intersections.
Check if alternate interior angles are equal.
State your conclusion clearly: 'Since the alternate angles are equal (both 65 degrees), the lines are parallel'.

callouts.p: A proof question is never finished with just a number. You must write a concluding sentence linking your numerical result back to the geometric property.

analogy.p: Think of congruent shapes as identical twin siblings: they wear the exact same clothes, have the same height, and match in every single way (Congruence = SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS). Think of similar shapes as a photo printed in two different sizes, or a model car and a real car: the doors open in the same places and the headlights are the same shape, but one is bigger than the other (Similarity = same angles, proportional sides).

terms.d: Identical in shape and size; corresponding sides and angles are equal.
Having the same shape with equal corresponding angles and proportional side lengths.
The ratio by which all linear dimensions of a shape are enlarged or reduced.
Side, Side, Side; a congruence criterion where all three pairs of corresponding sides are equal.
Side, Angle, Side; congruence criterion with two sides and the included angle equal.
Angle, Side, Angle; congruence criterion with two angles and the included side equal.
Right-angle, Hypotenuse, Side; congruence criterion for right-angled triangles.
A logical argument establishing the truth of a geometric statement using accepted definitions and theorems.
Angles on opposite sides of a transversal line crossing two parallel lines, forming a Z shape.
Angles in matching corners when a transversal crosses parallel lines, forming an F shape.
Angles inside parallel lines on the same side of a transversal, summing to 180 degrees (C shape).
The angle formed precisely between two given sides of a polygon or triangle.

mistakes.w: Saying triangles are congruent because all three angles are equal (AAA).
mistakes.r: AAA proves similarity, not congruence. Triangles can be different sizes.

mistakes.w: Using SSA or ASS as a congruence criterion.
mistakes.r: SSA / ASS is not a valid congruence rule because it can form two different triangles.

mistakes.w: Subtracting instead of multiplying when applying a scale factor to find a missing side.
mistakes.r: Similar shapes are scaled using multiplication or division by the scale factor, never addition or subtraction.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to write reasons in angle proof questions.
mistakes.r: Marks are specifically awarded for stating geometric reasons in brackets.

mistakes.w: Assuming shapes are similar just because they are both rectangles.
mistakes.r: Rectangles are only similar if the ratio of their width to height is identical.

mistakes.w: Mixing up vertex order when writing congruence statements.
mistakes.r: Corresponding vertices must match in exact sequence, e.g., triangle ABC congruent to triangle PQR.

mistakes.w: Using the scale factor for area when asked for a length.
mistakes.r: Length scale factor must be kept linear for side length calculations.

exam.q: Triangle A and Triangle B are congruent. Triangle A has sides 5 cm, 7 cm, and 10 cm. Write down the side lengths of Triangle B.
exam.tip: Congruent means identical in every way, so side lengths do not change.

exam.q: State the condition that proves two right-angled triangles are congruent when their hypotenuses and one other side are equal.
exam.tip: Memorise the four strict abbreviations: SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS.

exam.q: Two similar rectangles have lengths 4 cm and 12 cm. The width of the smaller rectangle is 3 cm. Calculate the width of the larger rectangle.
exam.tip: Always find the scale factor first by dividing the larger known side by the smaller known side.

exam.q: Explain why AAA is not a valid condition for triangle congruence.
model: AAA only proves the triangles are similar
They can be different sizes while having the same angles
exam.tip: Keep your explanation concise, focusing on size versus shape.

exam.q: Triangle PQR has angles 40° and 60°. Triangle XYZ has angles 40° and 80°. Are the two triangles similar? Explain your answer.
model: Yes, because all three corresponding angles are equal (AAA)
exam.tip: Always calculate the missing angle in a triangle before deciding on similarity.

exam.q: Triangle ABC has AB = 6 cm, AC = 8 cm, and angle BAC = 50°. Triangle DEF has DE = 6 cm, DF = 8 cm, and angle EDF = 50°. Are triangles ABC and DEF congruent? Give a reason.
model: SAS (Side, Angle, Side) because two sides and the included angle are equal
exam.tip: Check that the angle is strictly between the two given sides to confirm SAS.

exam.q: A model of a building is made to a scale of 1:20. The height of the model is 15 cm. Calculate the actual height of the building in meters.
model: Convert cm to m by dividing by 100
exam.tip: Watch out for unit conversions at the end of scale drawing and similarity questions.

exam.q: Two similar jugs have heights 10 cm and 15 cm. The surface area of the smaller jug is 40 cm². A student says the surface area of the larger jug is 60 cm². Explain why the student is wrong.
model: The student multiplied by the linear scale factor (1.5) instead of squaring it
Area scale factor is 1.5 squared = 2.25, so area is 40 x 2.25 = 90 cm²
exam.tip: Remember that length scale factor is k, area scale factor is k squared, and volume scale factor is k cubed.

exam.q: In a triangle, line DE is drawn parallel to base BC. Angle ADE = 40°. Write down the size of angle ABC and state the geometric reason.
exam.tip: Look out for F-shapes and Z-shapes formed by parallel lines in triangles.

exam.q: Prove that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal by splitting the triangle with an angle bisector.
model: Draw an angle bisector from the apex to the base
Two triangles are formed sharing the bisector line
The triangles are congruent by SAS (two sides and included angle equal)
Therefore, the base angles are equal because corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal
exam.tip: Lay out your proof in clear, numbered steps mentioning sides, angles, and criteria.

worked.q: Triangle A and Triangle B are similar. Triangle A has sides 4 cm, 6 cm, and 8 cm. The shortest side of Triangle B is 10 cm. Find the lengths of the other two sides of Triangle B.
steps: Identify corresponding sides: the shortest side of A is 4 cm, and the shortest side of B is 10 cm.
Calculate the linear scale factor = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5.
Multiply the remaining sides of Triangle A by the scale factor 2.5. Medium side: 6 x 2.5 = 15 cm.
Longest side: 8 x 2.5 = 20 cm.

worked.q: A vertical pole of height 3 m casts a shadow of 1.2 m. At the same time, a nearby tree casts a shadow of 4 m. Calculate the height of the tree.
steps: Set up the similarity ratio between the pole and the tree: Height ÷ Shadow = Scale Factor.
Scale factor for shadows = 4 ÷ 1.2 = 3.333... or keep as fraction 40/12 = 10/3.
Multiply the pole's height by the shadow ratio: 3 x (10 / 3) = 10.
Alternatively, set up a direct proportion equation: Height of tree ÷ 4 = 3 ÷ 1.2.

maths_aqa_f.3.13.summary: This revision module covers the essential area and volume calculations required for Foundation tier, focusing on triangles, parallelograms, trapezia, and standard 3D prisms and cylinders. You will learn to identify perpendicular heights, apply standard formulas accurately, and track units from millimetres to cubic metres. Mastering these methods ensures full marks on both calculator and non-calculator papers.

core.p: The area of any triangle is calculated by multiplying its base by its perpendicular height and dividing the result by 2. It is vital that the height used forms a 90-degree angle with the chosen base, rather than using a slanted side length.
bullets: Formula: Area = 0.5 × base × perpendicular height
The base and height must be perpendicular (meet at right angles)
Slanted side lengths (hypotenuse or legs) must never be used as the height
Always include correct squared units, such as cm² or m²

callouts.p: Always look for the dashed line showing a right angle symbol. That is your height.
Do not multiply the two given side lengths of a non-right-angled triangle together.

fig.cap: A triangle showing base b and perpendicular height h meeting at a right angle.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><polygon points="80,200 320,200 200,60" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="60" x2="200" y2="200" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4"/><rect x="200" y="180" width="20" height="20" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="190" y="135" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">h</text><text x="195" y="220" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Base (b)</text></svg>

core.p: A parallelogram has opposite sides that are parallel and equal in length. Its area is found by multiplying the base by the perpendicular height. Notice how slicing a triangle off one side and moving it to the other turns a parallelogram into a rectangle.
bullets: Formula: Area = base × perpendicular height
Written compactly as Area = b × h
The height is the vertical distance between the two parallel bases
Do not use the length of the slanted side in your area calculation

callouts.p: Think of a parallelogram as a rectangle that has been pushed sideways; the area rule remains base times height.

fig.cap: A parallelogram showing base b and perpendicular height h drawn outside or inside.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><polygon points="100,180 300,180 340,90 140,90" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="140" y1="90" x2="140" y2="180" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4"/><rect x="140" y="160" width="20" height="20" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="125" y="140" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">h</text><text x="210" y="200" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Base (b)</text></svg>

core.p: A trapezium is a four-sided shape with one pair of parallel sides. To find its area, add the lengths of the two parallel sides together, multiply by the perpendicular distance between them, and divide by 2.
bullets: Formula: Area = 0.5 × (a + b) × h
Variables a and b represent the two parallel sides
Variable h represents the perpendicular height between a and b
Always add a and b first before multiplying by h and dividing by 2

callouts.p: Calculate (a + b) first, then multiply by h, then multiply by 0.5 (or divide by 2).

fig.cap: A trapezium with parallel sides a and b, and perpendicular height h.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><polygon points="120,180 320,180 270,80 170,80" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="170" y1="80" x2="170" y2="180" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4"/><rect x="170" y="160" width="20" height="20" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="210" y="70" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Top side (a)</text><text x="200" y="200" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Bottom side (b)</text><text x="150" y="135" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">h</text></svg>

core.p: A prism is a 3D solid that has the exact same cross-section all the way along its length. If you slice right through a prism parallel to its end face, every single cross-section is identical in shape and size.
bullets: Key feature: Uniform cross-section along its entire length
Examples of prisms: Cuboids, triangular prisms, cylinders
Non-examples: Spheres, cones, pyramids (their cross-sections change size)
The volume is calculated using the cross-sectional area and the length

callouts.p: A solid geometric figure with two end faces that are similar, equal, and parallel rectilinear figures, and sides that are parallelograms.

core.p: The general formula to find the volume of any prism is wonderfully straightforward once you know the area of its end face. You simply multiply the area of the uniform cross-section by the length (or height) of the prism.
bullets: Formula: Volume = Area of cross-section × length
Written as V = A × l
Units for volume are always cubed, such as cm³ or m³
If the cross-section area is not given, calculate it first using area formulas

callouts.p: Step 1: Find the cross-sectional area. Step 2: Multiply by the length of the prism.

core.p: A cylinder is a special type of prism where the cross-section is a circle. Because the area of a circle is calculated using pi times radius squared, the volume formula for a cylinder adapts directly from the general prism rule.
bullets: Formula: Volume = π × r² × h (where r is radius, h is length/height)
Make sure you use the radius, not the diameter, in the formula
If given the diameter, divide by 2 first to find the radius
Leave answers in terms of π if requested, or give decimal answers to required accuracy

callouts.p: A common exam error is putting the diameter directly into r squared instead of halving it first.

fig.cap: A cylinder showing radius r and height h.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><ellipse cx="200" cy="70" rx="60" ry="25" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M140,70 L140,170 A60,25 0 0,0 260,170 L260,70" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="70" x2="260" y2="70" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2"/><text x="220" y="60" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">r</text><text x="275" y="125" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">h</text></svg>

core.p: Some exam questions ask for the volume of a shape made by joining two prisms together, or an L-shaped prism. To solve these, split the uniform cross-section into simpler shapes, find their individual areas, and sum them up before multiplying by the length.
bullets: Decompose the complex cross-section into rectangles, triangles, or trapezia
Find the total area of the cross-section
Multiply the total cross-sectional area by the prism's length
Alternatively, find the volume of each block separately and add them together

callouts.p: Always double-check missing lengths on composite shapes by checking opposite parallel sides.

core.h: Working Backwards: Finding a Missing Length
core.p: Examiners love testing if you can work in reverse. If you are given the volume of a prism and its cross-sectional area, you can rearrange the formula to find the missing length or height.
bullets: Formula rearrangement: Length = Volume ÷ Area of cross-section
If given the volume and length, find the cross-sectional area: Area = Volume ÷ Length
Check that all units match before performing division
Show all working clearly to pick up method marks even if arithmetic slips

callouts.p: Volume = Area × Length, so Length = Volume ÷ Area.

core.h: Unit Conversions for Area and Volume
core.p: Converting units for area and volume is very different from converting simple linear lengths. Because you are multiplying dimensions, the scaling factors change drastically and catch out unprepared students.
bullets: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 1 cm² = 10mm × 10mm = 100 mm²
1 cm = 10 mm, so 1 cm³ = 10mm × 10mm × 10mm = 1,000 mm³

callouts.p: Do not just multiply by 10 when converting cm² to mm². You must multiply by 10² = 100.

core.h: Exam Strategy for Area and Volume
core.p: Maxing your marks in geometry questions requires disciplined layout and careful attention to detail. Follow a strict routine of writing down formulas, substituting values, and verifying units.
bullets: Always write down the standard formula before substituting numbers
Show clear working steps for method marks
Check whether the question asks for pi to be left in the answer or evaluated as a decimal
Verify your final unit labels (cm for length, cm² for area, cm³ for volume)

callouts.p: Even if your calculator button slip leads to a wrong final answer, writing the formula scores vital method marks.

analogy.p: Imagine a freshly baked loaf of sliced sandwich bread. Each individual slice has the exact same face area. If you want to know the total volume of bread, you take the area of one single slice and multiply it by how many slices deep the loaf goes (its length). This is precisely how a prism works: volume is just stacking identical cross-sectional slices along a length. Where the analogy breaks down is that a loaf of bread usually tapers slightly at the crust ends, whereas a mathematical prism maintains 100% geometric uniformity along its entire extrusion.

terms.d: The measure of the amount of space inside a 2D flat shape, measured in square units.
The amount of 3D space enclosed by a solid object, measured in cubic units.
A straight line height that meets the base at exactly 90 degrees.
The 2D shape exposed when cutting straight through a 3D object parallel to its end face.
A 3D solid with a constant cross-section along its entire length.
A prism with a circular cross-section, two parallel circular bases, and a curved surface.
A quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides.
A quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides and equal opposite angles.
The distance from the exact centre of a circle to any point on its circumference.
A straight line passing completely through the centre of a circle, touching both sides.
The mathematical constant representing the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, approximately 3.14159.
Remaining constant, identical, and unchanging in form or size throughout.

mistakes.w: Multiplying the two slanted side lengths of a triangle to find its area.
mistakes.r: Always use base times perpendicular height divided by 2.

mistakes.w: Using the diameter instead of the radius in circle and cylinder calculations.
mistakes.r: Always divide the diameter by 2 to find the radius before applying πr².

mistakes.w: Forgetting to divide by 2 when calculating the area of a triangle or trapezium.
mistakes.r: Triangles include 0.5 × base × height; trapezia include halving the sum of parallel sides.

mistakes.w: Converting cm² to mm² by multiplying by 10.
mistakes.r: Area scale factors are squared, so multiply by 10² = 100.

mistakes.w: Adding the parallel sides of a trapezium instead of multiplying by height.
mistakes.r: Add parallel sides first, multiply by height, then divide by 2.

mistakes.w: Confusing surface area with volume for prisms.
mistakes.r: Volume is cross-sectional area multiplied by length; surface area is the total area of all outer faces.

mistakes.w: Using a slant height of a parallelogram as its perpendicular height.
mistakes.r: Ensure the height used forms a 90-degree right angle with the chosen base.

exam.q: Calculate the area of a triangle with base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm.
exam.tip: Always state units as cm² for area.

exam.q: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 12 m and perpendicular height 4.5 m.
exam.tip: Do not divide by 2 for a parallelogram.

exam.q: Calculate the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 7 cm and 11 cm, and perpendicular height 6 cm.
exam.tip: Add the parallel sides first inside brackets.

exam.q: Work out the volume of a triangular prism where the cross-sectional area is 24 cm² and the length is 10 cm.
exam.tip: Volume of a prism is cross-section area multiplied by length.

exam.q: A cylinder has a radius of 4 cm and a height of 10 cm. Calculate its volume to 1 decimal place.
exam.tip: Remember to square the radius before multiplying by height and pi.

exam.q: Convert 4.5 m² into cm².
exam.tip: Area conversion factor is 10,000, not 100.

exam.q: The volume of a cuboid is 180 cm³. Its cross-sectional base area is 15 cm². Find its length.
exam.tip: Rearrange Volume = Area × Length to find Length = Volume ÷ Area.

exam.q: A cylinder has a diameter of 10 cm and a height of 12 cm. Find its volume in terms of π.
exam.tip: Always halve the diameter first to get the radius.

exam.q: Calculate the area of a triangle with sides 6 cm, 8 cm, and 10 cm, where the sides of 6 cm and 8 cm meet at a right angle.
model: Identify base = 6 and height = 8 (or vice versa)
exam.tip: Ignore the hypotenuse (10 cm) when calculating the area of a right-angled triangle.

worked.q: Find the volume of a cylinder with diameter 14 cm and height 20 cm. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
steps: Step 1: Find the radius by dividing the diameter by 2. Radius r = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm.
Step 2: State the formula for the volume of a cylinder: Volume = π × r² × h.
Step 3: Substitute the values into the formula: Volume = π × 7² × 20.
Step 4: Calculate the exact value: π × 49 × 20 = 980π.
Step 5: Evaluate to decimal form and round to 3 significant figures: 980 × 3.14159... = 3078.76..., which rounds to 3080 cm³.

worked.q: A trapezium has parallel sides of length 8 cm and 12 cm. Its perpendicular height is 5 cm. This trapezium is the cross-section of a prism of length 15 cm. Calculate the total volume of the prism.
steps: Step 1: Find the area of the trapezium cross-section using Area = 0.5 × (a + b) × h.
Step 2: Substitute parallel sides and height: Area = 0.5 × (8 + 12) × 5.
Step 3: Compute the bracket sum: 8 + 12 = 20.
Step 4: Complete area calculation: 0.5 × 20 × 5 = 50 cm².
Step 5: Multiply cross-sectional area by the length of the prism: Volume = 50 × 15 = 750 cm³.

maths_aqa_f.3.14.summary: Mastering composite shapes, circles, and 3D surface area and volume is essential for top marks at Foundation tier. This guide covers circles, prisms, cylinders, spheres, cones, pyramids, and frustums with exact formulas and step-by-step methods. You will learn to break complex shapes into simpler parts, substitute values accurately, and maintain correct units throughout every calculation.

core.p: Circles are fundamental geometric shapes defined by a constant distance from the centre to any point on the boundary. To score top marks, you must distinguish clearly between circumference (perimeter) and area, using the correct mathematical constant pi.
bullets: Circumference formula: C = pi * d or C = 2 * pi * r
Area formula: A = pi * r^2
Diameter is always twice the radius: d = 2r
Always check whether the question asks for exact values in terms of pi or a decimal rounded to a specific number of decimal places or significant figures

callouts.p: A straight line segment from the centre of a circle to any point on its circumference.
Students frequently use the diameter instead of the radius in the area formula A = pi * r^2. Always find the radius first if given the diameter.

fig.cap: A circle showing radius r, diameter d passing through the centre, and circumference C around the edge.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><circle cx="200" cy="120" r="80" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="120" x2="280" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="120" y1="120" x2="280" y2="120" stroke="#ef4444" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4"/><circle cx="200" cy="120" r="4" fill="#1b2540"/><text x="235" y="112" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Radius r</text><text x="180" y="105" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Centre</text><text x="145" y="140" fill="ef4444" font-size="12">Diameter d</text></svg>

core.p: Composite shapes are made by joining two or more standard shapes together. To find the total area or perimeter, you must split the composite shape into familiar shapes like rectangles, triangles, and semicircles.
bullets: Split compound shapes using dashed construction lines
Calculate the area of each individual section separately
Add the individual areas together for total area, or subtract if a region is cut out
For perimeter, sum only the outer boundaries and exclude internal dividing lines

callouts.p: Never add internal lines when calculating the perimeter of a composite shape. Perimeter is strictly the distance all the way around the outside.
Remember that the area of a semicircle is (pi * r^2) / 2 and its curved boundary is (pi * d) / 2 plus the straight diameter.

fig.cap: A composite shape formed by a rectangle and a semicircle on top, showing separated dimensions.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="120" y="120" width="160" height="80" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 120 120 A 80 80 0 0 1 280 120 Z" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="120" y1="220" x2="280" y2="220" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="190" y="235" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">10 cm</text><text x="180" y="165" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Rectangle</text><text x="180" y="90" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Semicircle</text></svg>

core.h: Volume and Surface Area of Cylinders
core.p: A cylinder is a 3D prism with circular cross-sections. Its volume and surface area formulas are derived from the area of the circular ends and the curved rectangular wall when unrolled.
bullets: Volume of a cylinder: V = pi * r^2 * h (Cross-sectional area multiplied by length)
Curved surface area: CSA = 2 * pi * r * h
Total surface area: TSA = 2 * pi * r^2 + 2 * pi * r * h (Includes two circular ends)
Ensure radius and height are in the same units before calculating

callouts.p: A uniform slice taken parallel to the circular base; every cross-section of a cylinder is identical.

fig.cap: A cylinder showing radius r and height h.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><ellipse cx="200" cy="70" rx="50" ry="20" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 150 70 L 150 170 A 50 20 0 0 0 250 170 L 250 70" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="70" x2="250" y2="70" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="260" y1="70" x2="260" y2="170" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="215" y="60" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">r</text><text x="270" y="125" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">h</text></svg>

core.h: Volume and Surface Area of Spheres
core.p: Spheres are perfectly round 3D objects where every point on the surface is equidistant from the centre. AQA Foundation tier supplies the formulas in the exam paper, but you must know how to substitute into them correctly.
bullets: Volume of a sphere: V = (4/3) * pi * r^3
Surface area of a sphere: SA = 4 * pi * r^2
Identify whether you are given the radius or the diameter
Cube the radius for volume (r^3) and square the radius for surface area (r^2)

callouts.p: A very common error is using r^2 for volume and r^3 for surface area. Memorise: Volume is cubed (3D units cm^3), surface area is squared (2D units cm^2).

core.h: Volume and Surface Area of Pyramids
core.p: Pyramids have a flat polygonal base and triangular faces that meet at a single point called the apex. The volume formula applies to any pyramid regardless of the shape of its base.
bullets: Volume of a pyramid: V = (1/3) * base area * perpendicular height
Surface area: Sum of the area of the base and the areas of all triangular side faces
Perpendicular height is the vertical distance from the apex straight down to the centre of the base
Slant height is needed for finding the area of the triangular faces

callouts.p: Always ensure you use the perpendicular height in the volume formula, never the sloping edge length of the pyramid.

core.h: Volume and Surface Area of Cones
core.p: A cone is a circular-based pyramid with a curved sloping surface rising to an apex. To find surface area and volume, you need the radius, vertical height, and slant height.
bullets: Volume of a cone: V = (1/3) * pi * r^2 * h
Curved surface area: CSA = pi * r * l (where l is the slant height)
Total surface area: TSA = pi * r * l + pi * r^2
Use Pythagoras theorem on the vertical cross-section to find l, r, or h if one is missing: l^2 = r^2 + h^2

callouts.p: The vertical height, radius, and slant height form a right-angled triangle inside the cone. Use a^2 + b^2 = c^2 whenever you need the slant height l.

core.h: Volume and Surface Area of Frustums
core.p: A frustum is created when you slice the top off a cone or pyramid parallel to its base. Frustum calculations require proportional reasoning or subtracting the removed small cone from the original large cone.
bullets: Volume of frustum = Volume of large cone - Volume of small removed cone
Curved surface area = CSA of large cone - CSA of small removed cone
Identify the scaling factor between the large and small cones when given similar shapes
Add the remaining base area if calculating total surface area

callouts.p: The portion of a solid cone or pyramid that lies between two parallel planes cutting through it.

core.p: When converting between units of length, area, and volume, the scaling factors change. A common exam trap is converting linear units incorrectly when working with volume.
bullets: Length conversion: 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m
Area conversion: 1 cm^2 = 10^2 mm^2 = 100 mm^2
Volume conversion: 1 cm^3 = 10^3 mm^3 = 1000 mm^3
1 litre = 1000 cm^3 (vital conversion for capacity questions)

callouts.p: To convert cm^3 to m^3, divide by 1,000,000 (100^3), not 100!

analogy.p: Think of finding volume as filling a room with identical small boxes (cubes of space), where every extra dimension multiplies the capacity. Surface area is like wrapping Christmas presents: you only care about covering the outside skin, measuring each panel flat before taping them together. Pyramids and cones taper to a point, which is why their volume formulas include a third (1/3), as they take up less space than a straight-sided prism or cylinder of the same base and height.

terms.d: The distance from the centre of a circle to any point on its circumference.
A straight line passing through the centre of a circle touching both sides of the circumference.
The perimeter or boundary distance around a circle.
The mathematical constant approximately equal to 3.14159, representing the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
A shape made up of two or more geometric shapes combined together.
A 3D solid with identical cross-sections all along its length.
The face created when a 3D solid is cut parallel to its base.
A 3D solid with two parallel circular bases connected by a curved surface.
A perfectly round 3D geometrical object where every point on the surface is equidistant from the centre.
A 3D shape with a polygonal base and triangular faces meeting at a common apex.
A 3D solid with a circular base tapering smoothly to a point called the apex.
The length measured along the sloping outer surface of a cone or pyramid from base to apex.
The remaining part of a cone or pyramid after the top has been sliced off by a plane parallel to the base.

mistakes.w: Using the diameter instead of the radius in circle area or volume formulas
mistakes.r: Always halve the diameter first to find the radius before squaring or cubing.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the factor of 1/3 for cones and pyramids
mistakes.r: Remember that pointed 3D shapes have 1/3 the volume of corresponding prisms/cylinders.

mistakes.w: Adding internal boundaries when calculating the perimeter of a composite shape
mistakes.r: Perimeter is strictly the outer boundary distance only.

mistakes.w: Using vertical height instead of slant height when finding the curved surface area of a cone
mistakes.r: Curved surface area of a cone uses pi * r * l, where l is the slant height.

mistakes.w: Confusing volume units with linear conversions (e.g. dividing by 100 to convert cm^3 to m^3)
mistakes.r: Cube the linear conversion factor: 1 m^3 = 1,000,000 cm^3.

mistakes.w: Writing answers without units or with incorrect square/cube units
mistakes.r: Area is cm^2, volume is cm^3, length is cm.

mistakes.w: Rounding intermediate steps in multi-step volume calculations
mistakes.r: Keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer, then round as requested.

exam.q: Calculate the circumference of a circle with a diameter of 14 cm. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
exam.tip: Remember to round correctly to 1 decimal place.

exam.q: Work out the area of a semicircle with radius 6 cm. Give your answer in terms of pi.
model: Area of full circle = pi * 6^2 = 36 * pi
exam.tip: In terms of pi means leave pi in your final answer.

exam.q: A cylinder has radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. Calculate its volume. Use pi = 3.142.
exam.tip: Substitute carefully into the formula provided in the exam paper.

exam.q: Calculate the volume of a sphere with radius 5 cm. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
exam.tip: Check significant figure rounding rules carefully.

exam.q: A square-based pyramid has a base of side length 6 cm and a perpendicular height of 10 cm. Calculate its volume.
exam.tip: Find the area of the base first before applying the 1/3 formula.

exam.q: A cone has a base radius of 5 cm and a slant height of 13 cm. Calculate the total surface area of the cone in terms of pi.
model: Curved surface area = pi * r * l = pi * 5 * 13 = 65pi
exam.tip: Total surface area includes both the curved side and the circular base.

exam.q: Convert 4.5 m^3 into cubic centimetres (cm^3).
exam.tip: Cube the scale factor 100 when converting volume units.

exam.q: Work out the perimeter of a running track shape made from a rectangle of length 20 m and width 10 m, with semicircles at both ends.
model: Two semicircles with diameter 10 m make one full circle of circumference C = pi * 10 = 31.415...
Add the two straight lengths of the rectangle: 20 + 20 = 40
exam.tip: Two identical semicircles combine to form one full circle.

exam.q: A solid metal cylinder has a radius of 3 cm and a height of 8 cm. Calculate the total surface area of the cylinder. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
exam.tip: Remember a cylinder has two circular ends, top and bottom.

exam.q: Calculate the volume of a frustum formed by removing a cone of radius 2 cm and height 3 cm from a larger cone of radius 6 cm and height 9 cm.
exam.tip: Frustum volume is always large solid minus small removed solid.

worked.q: Calculate the volume of a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 15 cm. Take pi = 3.142.
steps: Identify the formula for the volume of a cylinder: V = pi * r^2 * h
Substitute the given values into the formula: V = 3.142 * 7^2 * 15
Calculate the squared radius: 7^2 = 49

worked.q: Find the total surface area of a sphere with a diameter of 12 cm. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
steps: Find the radius by dividing the diameter by 2: r = 12 / 2 = 6 cm
Identify the surface area formula for a sphere: SA = 4 * pi * r^2
Substitute the radius: SA = 4 * pi * 6^2 = 4 * pi * 36 = 144 * pi
Calculate decimal value: 144 * 3.14159... = 452.389...
Round to 1 decimal place: 452.4
